question: A 72-year-old male visits his gastroenterologist for a check-up one year following resection of a 2-cm malignant lesion in his sigmoid colon. Serum levels of which of the following can be used in this patient to test for cancer recurrence?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Resection of malignant lesion in sigmoid colon" -> "risk of cancer recurrence" -> "need for monitoring serum tumor markers" -> "Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is associated with colorectal cancer" -> "elevated CEA levels indicate possible recurrence" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Colorectal cancer history" -> "monitoring for recurrence is essential" -> "Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is a standard marker" -> "elevated CEA levels suggest recurrence" -> 90%

CHAIN: "Patient with previous sigmoid colon cancer" -> "serum markers are useful for recurrence detection" -> "Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is relevant for colorectal cancer" -> "increased CEA levels may indicate cancer recurrence" -> 80%
CHAIN: "Post-surgical follow-up for colon cancer" -> "need to assess for recurrence" -> "Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is commonly used" -> "high CEA levels can signal recurrence" -> 90%
analysis: In this case, the patient has a history of a malignant lesion in the sigmoid colon, which suggests a potential for colorectal cancer recurrence. Among the options provided, Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is a well-established tumor marker used to monitor colorectal cancer. Elevated levels of CEA can indicate recurrence of the disease. Alpha-fetoprotein is primarily associated with liver cancer and germ cell tumors, CA-125 is mainly used for ovarian cancer, CA-19-9 is associated with pancreatic cancer, and gamma-glutamyl transferase is a liver enzyme not specific for cancer. Therefore, CEA is the most relevant marker for this patient to assess for cancer recurrence.
